claim: During meiosis, a single round of DNA replication is followed by two consecutive rounds of nuclear divisions called meiosis I and meiosis II.
source: During meiosis, a single round of DNA replication is followed by two consecutive rounds of nuclear divisions called meiosis I and meiosis II.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cell biology and represents established scientific knowledge about meiosis.

claim: In meiosis I, homologous chromosomes segregate, while sister chromatids remain together.
source: In meiosis I, homologous chromosomes segregate, while sister chromatids remain together.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the meiosis I division pattern.

claim: Preventing microtubule–kinetochore interactions during premeiotic S phase and prophase I is essential for establishing the meiosis I chromosome segregation pattern.
source: Here we show that preventing microtubule–kinetochore interactions during premeiotic S phase and prophase I is essential for establishing the meiosis I chromosome segregation pattern.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Premature interactions of kinetochores with microtubules transform meiosis I into a mitosis-like division.
source: Premature interactions of kinetochores with microtubules transform meiosis I into a mitosis-like division by disrupting two key meiosis I events: coorientation of sister kinetochores and protection of centromeric cohesin removal from chromosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that premature microtubule-kinetochore interactions lead to sister chromatid segregation in meiosis I.

claim: Premature microtubule–kinetochore interactions disrupt coorientation of sister kinetochores.
source: Premature interactions of kinetochores with microtubules transform meiosis I into a mitosis-like division by disrupting two key meiosis I events: coorientation of sister kinetochores and protection of centromeric cohesin removal from chromosomes.
evidence: This is supported by data showing monopolin localization defects in CUP-CLB3 cells (Figure 3).

claim: Premature microtubule–kinetochore interactions disrupt protection of centromeric cohesin removal from chromosomes.
source: Premature interactions of kinetochores with microtubules transform meiosis I into a mitosis-like division by disrupting two key meiosis I events: coorientation of sister kinetochores and protection of centromeric cohesin removal from chromosomes.
evidence: This is supported by data showing loss of centromeric Rec8 in CUP-CLB3 cells (Figure 4).

claim: Restricting outer kinetochore assembly contributes to preventing premature engagement of microtubules with kinetochores.
source: Furthermore we find that restricting outer kinetochore assembly contributes to preventing premature engagement of microtubules with kinetochores.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that outer kinetochore components like Ndc80 and Hsk3 are downregulated during prophase I (Figure 6).

claim: Inhibition of microtubule–kinetochore interactions during premeiotic S phase and prophase I is central to establishing the unique meiosis I chromosome segregation pattern.
source: We propose that inhibition of microtubule–kinetochore interactions during premeiotic S phase and prophase I is central to establishing the unique meiosis I chromosome segregation pattern.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Reciprocal recombination between homologous chromosomes is required to establish the specialized chromosome segregation pattern in meiosis.
source: The establishment of this specialized chromosome segregation pattern requires three changes that modulate how chromosomes interact with each other and with the microtubule cytoskeleton: (1) reciprocal recombination between homologous chromosomes, (2) the way linkages between sister chromatids, known as sister-chromatid cohesion, are removed from chromosomes and (3) the manner in which chromosomes attach to the meiotic spindle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about meiosis, cited in the introduction.

claim: Homologous recombination is initiated by programmed double-strand breaks (DSBs), which are catalyzed by Spo11 following premeiotic DNA replication.
source: Homologous recombination is initiated by programmed double-strand breaks (DSBs), which are catalyzed by Spo11 following premeiotic DNA replication (Keeney et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Keeney et al., 1997.

claim: Crossover recombination generates physical linkages between homologous chromosomes.
source: Subsequent repair of DSBs by crossover recombination generates physical linkages between homologous chromosomes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about meiotic recombination.

claim: The spindle assembly checkpoint prevents the onset of chromosome segregation until biorientation is completed.
source: The spindle assembly checkpoint prevents the onset of chromosome segregation until this process is completed.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the spindle assembly checkpoint function.

claim: The anaphase promoting complex/cyclosome and its specificity factor Cdc20 (APC/C-Cdc20) targets Securin for degradation.
source: A ubiquitin ligase known as the anaphase promoting complex/cyclosome and its specificity factor Cdc20 (APC/C-Cdc20) targets Securin for degradation, relieving Separase inhibition (Cohen-Fix et al., 1996; Ciosk et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cohen-Fix et al., 1996 and Ciosk et al., 1998.

claim: Separase is a protease that cleaves the kleisin subunit of cohesin.
source: Separase is a protease that cleaves the kleisin subunit of cohesin, the protein complex that mediates sister-chromatid cohesion (Uhlmann et al., 1999, 2000; Schleiffer et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Uhlmann et al., 1999, 2000 and Schleiffer et al., 2003.

claim: In meiosis I, cleavage of cohesin at chromosome arms allows homologs to segregate.
source: In meiosis I, cleavage of cohesin at chromosome arms allows homologs to segregate (Buonomo et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Buonomo et al., 2000.

claim: Cohesin around the centromeres is protected from cleavage during meiosis I, which is essential for the accurate segregation of sister chromatids during meiosis II.
source: However, cohesin around the centromeres is protected from cleavage during meiosis I, which is essential for the accurate segregation of sister chromatids during meiosis II.
evidence: This is established knowledge about meiotic cohesin regulation.

claim: Protection of centromeric cohesin is accomplished by preventing phosphorylation of Rec8, the meiosis-specific kleisin.
source: Protection of centromeric cohesin is accomplished by preventing phosphorylation of Rec8, the meiosis-specific kleisin. This occurs, at least in part, by Sgo1 (MEI-S332)-dependent recruitment of the protein phosphatase PP2A to centromeric regions where it antagonizes Rec8 phosphorylation (Kerrebrock et al., 1995; Katis et al., 2004a; Kitajima et al., 2004, 2006; Riedel et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on Sgo1 and PP2A function.

claim: In meiosis I, kinetochores of sister chromatid pairs attach to microtubules emanating from the same spindle pole, a process called sister kinetochore coorientation.
source: In meiosis I, kinetochores of sister chromatid pairs (henceforth sister kinetochores) attach to microtubules emanating from the same spindle pole, a process called sister kinetochore coorientation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about meiosis I kinetochore behavior.

claim: During meiosis II, sister kinetochores attach to microtubules emanating from opposite spindle poles and are thus bioriented.
source: During meiosis II, as during mitosis, sister kinetochores attach to microtubules emanating from opposite spindle poles and are thus bioriented (reviewed in Marston and Amon, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Marston and Amon, 2004.

claim: In budding yeast, sister kinetochore coorientation is brought about by the monopolin complex, which consists of Mam1, Lrs4, Csm1 and the casein kinase 1, Hrr25.
source: In budding yeast, sister kinetochore coorientation is brought about by the monopolin complex, which consists of Mam1, Lrs4, Csm1 and the casein kinase 1, Hrr25 (Toth et al., 2000; Rabitsch et al., 2003; Petronczki et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies identifying monopolin components.

claim: Lrs4 and Csm1 localize to the nucleolus during interphase.
source: Lrs4 and Csm1 localize to the nucleolus during interphase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about monopolin localization.

claim: During exit from pachytene, Lrs4 and Csm1 associate with Mam1 and Hrr25 at kinetochores, a process that requires the Polo kinase Cdc5.
source: During exit from pachytene, a stage of prophase I, Lrs4 and Csm1 associate with Mam1 and Hrr25 at kinetochores, a process that requires the Polo kinase Cdc5 (Clyne et al., 2003; Lee and Amon, 2003; Matos et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on monopolin kinetochore localization.

claim: In budding yeast, a single CDK associates with one of six B-type cyclins (Clb1-Clb6).
source: In budding yeast, a single CDK associates with one of six B-type cyclins (Clb1-Clb6) (reviewed in Morgan, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Morgan, 1997.

claim: In meiosis, Clb5- and Clb6-CDKs drive DNA replication and recombination, whereas Clb1-, Clb3- and Clb4-CDKs promote the meiotic nuclear divisions.
source: In meiosis, Clb5- and Clb6-CDKs drive DNA replication and recombination, whereas Clb1-, Clb3- and Clb4-CDKs promote the meiotic nuclear divisions (reviewed in Marston and Amon, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Marston and Amon, 2004.

claim: Meiotic cyclin-CDK activity is regulated both at the transcriptional and translational level.
source: Meiotic cyclin-CDK activity is regulated both at the transcriptional and translational level (Grandin and Reed, 1993; Carlile and Amon, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Grandin and Reed, 1993 and Carlile and Amon, 2008.

claim: Transcription of CLB1, CLB3 and CLB4 occurs only after exit from pachytene.
source: Transcription of CLB1, CLB3 and CLB4 occurs only after exit from pachytene (Chu and Herskowitz, 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chu and Herskowitz, 1998.

claim: CLB3 is translationally repressed during meiosis I, thus restricting Clb3-CDK activity to meiosis II.
source: CLB3 is also translationally repressed during meiosis I, thus restricting Clb3-CDK activity to meiosis II (Carlile and Amon, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carlile and Amon, 2008.

claim: The major mitotic cyclin, CLB2, is not expressed during meiosis.
source: The major mitotic cyclin, CLB2, is not expressed during meiosis (Grandin and Reed, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grandin and Reed, 1993.

claim: Expression of CLB3 from the GAL1-10 promoter leads to Clb3 accumulation in meiosis I to levels that are comparable to those seen in meiosis II in wild-type cells.
source: Expression from the GAL1-10 promoter led to Clb3 accumulation in meiosis I to levels that are comparable to those seen in meiosis II in wild-type cells (Carlile and Amon, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carlile and Amon, 2008.

claim: Estrogen interferes with meiotic progression when added during early stages of sporulation.
source: However, estrogen interferes with meiotic progression when added during early stages of sporulation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Expression from the CUP1 promoter led to approximately fivefold higher levels of Clb3 protein compared to expression from the GAL1-10 promoter.
source: Expression from the CUP1 promoter led to approximately fivefold higher levels of Clb3 protein compared to expression from the GAL1-10 promoter (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Despite the difference in Clb3 protein levels, the extent of sister chromatid segregation in meiosis I was similar between GAL-CLB3 and CUP-CLB3 cells.
source: The analysis of GFP dot segregation during the first meiotic division revealed that despite the difference in Clb3 protein levels, the extent of sister chromatid segregation in meiosis I was similar between GAL-CLB3 and CUP-CLB3 cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by GFP dot segregation data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The timing of when Clb3 is expressed, rather than the amount of Clb3 present, appears to be the primary determinant of sister chromatid segregation in meiosis I.
source: This finding indicates that expression of Clb3 from either the CUP1 or GAL1-10 promoter efficiently induces sister chromatid segregation during meiosis I. Furthermore, the timing of when Clb3 is expressed, rather than the amount of Clb3 present, appears to be the primary determinant of this phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that different Clb3 levels produce similar phenotypes.

claim: Expression of CLB1, CLB3 or CLB4 is sufficient to promote bipolar spindle assembly in NDT80-depleted cells.
source: We conclude that expression of CLB1, CLB3 or CLB4 is sufficient to promote bipolar spindle assembly in NDT80-depleted cells.
evidence: This is supported by data showing spindle formation in CUP-CLB1, CUP-CLB3, and CUP-CLB4 cells (Figure 2A).

claim: Expression of CLB5 from the CUP1 promoter did not lead to SPB separation and spindle formation in prophase I-arrested cells.
source: Expression of CLB5 from the CUP1 promoter did not lead to SPB separation and spindle formation either, although expression of CLB5 in the prophase I arrest led to a significant increase in total CDK activity (Figures 1F and 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1F, 2A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CUP-CLB1, CUP-CLB3 and CUP-CLB4 cells separated SPBs and formed bipolar spindles shortly after copper addition.
source: In contrast, CUP-CLB1, CUP-CLB3 and CUP-CLB4 cells separated SPBs and formed bipolar spindles, shortly after copper addition (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dynamic separation of heterozygous CENV-GFP dots was observed upon expression of CLB1 or CLB3, with sister kinetochores frequently splitting and coming together.
source: In contrast, we observed dynamic separation of heterozygous CENV-GFP dots upon expression of CLB1 or CLB3, with sister kinetochores frequently splitting and coming together (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Cells expressing CLB4 did not show transient splitting of sister kinetochores in prophase I.
source: Cells expressing CLB4 did not show transient splitting of sister kinetochores in prophase I, indicating that chromosomes are either unable to attach to the spindle or that homologous chromosomes, instead of sister chromatids, are bioriented as occurs in wild-type cells during metaphase I.
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data.

claim: In CUP-CLB4 cells, the two CENV-GFP dots remained tightly associated in prophase I, indicating that the homologous chromosomes are paired and not attached to the prematurely formed spindle.
source: Similar to wild-type, we observed that in CUP-CLB4 cells the two CENV-GFP dots remained tightly associated in prophase I, indicating that the homologous chromosomes are paired and not attached to the prematurely formed spindle (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: CUP-CLB1, CUP-CLB3 or CUP-CLB4 expression promotes bipolar spindle formation in pachytene-arrested cells, but only CLB1 and CLB3 expression can promote stable microtubule–kinetochore attachments sufficient to generate tension.
source: Together, these results indicate that CUP-CLB1, CUP-CLB3 or CUP-CLB4 expression promotes bipolar spindle formation in pachytene-arrested cells, but only CLB1 and CLB3 expression can promote stable microtubule–kinetochore attachments sufficient to generate tension.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only CLB1 and CLB3 induce sister kinetochore splitting.

claim: Expression of all four cyclins led to a significant increase in total CDK activity in prophase I.
source: Expression of all four cyclins led to a significant increase in total CDK activity in prophase I (Figure 1F)
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The degree of increase in CDK activity did not correlate with the ability to induce sister chromatid splitting in the NDT80 arrest.
source: but importantly, the degree of increase did not correlate with the ability to induce sister chromatid splitting in the NDT80 arrest.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing CDK activity levels with phenotypes.

claim: Clb1 expression led to a similar increase in Cdc28-associated kinase activity as expression of Clb4, yet Clb1 induced sister chromatid splitting whereas Clb4 did not.
source: For example, Clb1 expression led to a similar increase in Cdc28-associated kinase activity as expression of Clb4, yet Clb1 induced sister chromatid splitting whereas Clb4 did not (Figures 1F and 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1F and 2B,C.

claim: The ability to induce sister chromatid splitting does not correlate with total CDK activity produced by the various CUP-CLB fusions.
source: We conclude that the ability to induce sister chromatid splitting does not correlate with total CDK activity produced by the various CUP-CLB fusions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that similar CDK activity levels produce different phenotypes.

claim: SPB separation and spindle formation are not sufficient to induce microtubule–kinetochore interactions.
source: Furthermore, SPB separation and spindle formation are not sufficient to induce microtubule–kinetochore interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CUP-CLB4 cells form spindles but do not show sister kinetochore splitting.

claim: 39% of CUP-CLB1 and 41% of CUP-CLB3 cells segregated sister chromatids in the first division.
source: In contrast, 39% of CUP-CLB1 and 41% of CUP-CLB3 cells segregated sister chromatids in the first division, as judged by the presence of binucleate cells with a GFP dot in each nucleus (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by GFP dot segregation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In wild-type cells harboring heterozygous CENV-GFP dots, Pds1 degradation was immediately followed by movement of the single GFP dot to one side of the cell, indicating that homologous chromosomes had segregated.
source: In wild-type cells harboring heterozygous CENV-GFP dots, Pds1 degradation was immediately followed by movement of the single GFP dot to one side of the cell, indicating that homologous chromosomes had segregated.
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CUP-CLB3 cells segregated sister chromatids immediately after Pds1 degradation (median = 7 min after Pds1 degradation).
source: In contrast, CUP-CLB3 cells segregated sister chromatids immediately after Pds1 degradation (median = 7 min after Pds1 degradation; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CUP-CLB3 cells must be defective in two key aspects of meiosis I chromosome segregation: coorientation of sister kinetochores and maintenance of centromeric cohesion.
source: These results demonstrate that CUP-CLB3 cells segregate sister chromatids during the first meiotic division. Thus, CUP-CLB3 cells must be defective in two key aspects of meiosis I chromosome segregation: coorientation of sister kinetochores and maintenance of centromeric cohesion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that sister chromatids segregate in meiosis I.

claim: No major defects in DSB formation, synaptonemal complex assembly and generation of recombination products were observed in CUP-CLB3 cells.
source: We observed no major defects in DSB formation, synaptonemal complex assembly and generation of recombination products, nor did preventing homologous recombination affect the phenotypes caused by premature CLB3 expression (Figure 2—figure supplements 5–8).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 5–8.

claim: Preventing homologous recombination did not affect the phenotypes caused by premature CLB3 expression.
source: We observed no major defects in DSB formation, synaptonemal complex assembly and generation of recombination products, nor did preventing homologous recombination affect the phenotypes caused by premature CLB3 expression (Figure 2—figure supplements 5–8).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: Colocalization of Lrs4 or Mam1 with the kinetochore component Ndc10 was dramatically reduced in CUP-CLB3 but not CUP-CLB4 cells.
source: Colocalization of Lrs4 or Mam1 with the kinetochore component Ndc10 was dramatically reduced in CUP-CLB3 but not CUP-CLB4 cells (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by chromosome spread data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Hyperphosphorylation of Lrs4, which correlates with monopolin function, was significantly reduced in CUP-CLB3, but not in CUP-CLB4 cells.
source: Hyperphosphorylation of Lrs4, which correlates with monopolin function (Clyne et al., 2003; Lee and Amon, 2003; Matos et al., 2008), was also significantly reduced in CUP-CLB3, but not in CUP-CLB4 cells (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Premature expression of CLB3 prevents monopolin association with kinetochores.
source: These results indicate that premature expression of CLB3 prevents monopolin association with kinetochores.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that monopolin localization is defective in CUP-CLB3 cells.

claim: Association of both Rec8 and Pds5 with chromosomes in CUP-CLB3 cells was indistinguishable from that of wild-type cells during prophase I or metaphase I.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) and chromosome spreads revealed that association of both proteins with chromosomes in CUP-CLB3 cells was indistinguishable from that of wild-type cells during prophase I or metaphase I (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP and chromosome spread data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Loading of cohesion factors onto chromosomes is not affected in CUP-CLB3 cells.
source: Thus, loading of cohesion factors onto chromosomes is not affected in CUP-CLB3 cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Rec8 and Pds5 associate normally with chromosomes.

claim: Rec8 colocalized with the kinetochore component Ndc10 in binucleate wild-type and CUP-CLB4 cells.
source: Rec8 colocalized with the kinetochore component Ndc10 in binucleate wild-type and CUP-CLB4 cells, demonstrating that centromeric cohesin is protected from removal until the onset of anaphase II.
evidence: This is supported by chromosome spread data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Rec8 was not detected around centromeres in a substantial fraction of binucleate CUP-CLB3 cells.
source: In contrast, Rec8 was not detected around centromeres in a substantial fraction of binucleate CUP-CLB3 cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by chromosome spread data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: mam1∆ cells biorient sister chromatids during meiosis I but delay nuclear division until meiosis II due to the presence of centromeric cohesin.
source: Although mam1∆ cells biorient sister chromatids during meiosis I, they delay nuclear division until meiosis II due to the presence of centromeric cohesin (Toth et al., 2000; Rabitsch et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Toth et al., 2000 and Rabitsch et al., 2003.

claim: The delay in nuclear division of a mam1∆ was partially alleviated by the expression of CUP-CLB3.
source: The delay in nuclear division of a mam1∆ was partially alleviated by the expression of CUP-CLB3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Both centromeric and arm cohesin are lost from chromosomes at the onset of anaphase I in CUP-CLB3 cells.
source: We conclude that both centromeric and arm cohesin are lost from chromosomes at the onset of anaphase I in CUP-CLB3 cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Rec8 is lost from centromeres in CUP-CLB3 cells.

claim: Cleavage of cohesin by separase requires the phosphorylation of Rec8 at multiple residues.
source: Cleavage of cohesin by separase requires the phosphorylation of Rec8 at multiple residues (Brar et al., 2006; Katis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brar et al., 2006 and Katis et al., 2010.

claim: A recessive allele of REC8 in which 29 in vivo phosphorylation sites were mutated to alanine (rec8-29A) was not cleaved in CUP-CLB3 cells, but wild-type Rec8 was.
source: A recessive allele of REC8 in which 29 in vivo phosphorylation sites were mutated to alanine (rec8-29A) (Brar et al., 2006) was not cleaved in CUP-CLB3 cells, but wild-type Rec8 was (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The rec8-29A allele caused a similar metaphase I delay in wild-type and CUP-CLB3 cells when expressed as the sole source of REC8.
source: Furthermore, the rec8-29A allele caused a similar metaphase I delay in wild-type and CUP-CLB3 cells when expressed as the sole source of REC8 (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplements 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplements 5 and 6.

claim: Rec8 phosphorylation is required for cohesin removal in CUP-CLB3 cells.
source: Our results demonstrate that Rec8 phosphorylation is required for cohesin removal in CUP-CLB3 cells
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the rec8-29A allele prevents cohesin removal.

claim: The defect in centromeric cohesin protection in CUP-CLB3 cells may result from increased phosphorylation of centromeric Rec8.
source: and suggest that the defect in centromeric cohesin protection may result from increased phosphorylation of centromeric Rec8.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the requirement for Rec8 phosphorylation.

claim: The amount of phosphorylated Rec8 was increased at the centromere in CUP-CLB3 cells compared to wild-type cells.
source: However, the amount of phosphorylated Rec8 was increased at the centromere in CUP-CLB3 cells compared to wild-type cells, albeit not to the same extent as in cells depleted for Sgo1 (sgo1-mn), in which meiosis I centromeric-cohesin protection is completely defective (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data using phospho-specific antibodies shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CUP-CLB3 cells are compromised in preventing centromeric Rec8 phosphorylation during meiosis I.
source: We conclude that CUP-CLB3 cells are compromised in preventing centromeric Rec8 phosphorylation during meiosis I.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that centromeric Rec8 phosphorylation is increased.

claim: Sgo1, the PP2A regulatory subunit Rts1 and Spo13 localized normally in prophase I- and metaphase I-arrested CUP-CLB3 cells.
source: Surprisingly, Sgo1, the PP2A regulatory subunit Rts1 and Spo13 localized normally in prophase I- and metaphase I-arrested CUP-CLB3 cells (Figure 4F–H and Figure 4—figure supplements 7–9).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP and chromosome spread data shown in Figure 4F–H and Figure 4—figure supplements 7–9.

claim: A moderate reduction of Sgo1 and Rts1 at centromeres was observed in binucleate CUP-CLB3 cells.
source: We noticed a moderate reduction of Sgo1 and Rts1 at centromeres in binucleate CUP-CLB3 cells (Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 10).
evidence: This is supported by chromosome spread data shown in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 10.

claim: The reduction of Sgo1 and Rts1 during anaphase I is most likely a consequence rather than a cause of premature loss of centromeric cohesin.
source: However, this reduction during anaphase I is most likely a consequence rather than a cause of premature loss of centromeric cohesin.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Rts1 localization is also reduced in rec8-4D cells that lose centromeric cohesin.

claim: In cells expressing a phosphomimetic version of Rec8 (rec8-4D) that cannot be retained at centromeres beyond meiosis I, Rts1 localization is also reduced in anaphase I.
source: In cells expressing a phosphomimetic version of Rec8 (rec8-4D) that cannot be retained at centromeres beyond meiosis I, Rts1 localization is also reduced in anaphase I (Figure 4—figure supplement 11).
evidence: This is supported by chromosome spread data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 11.

claim: It is unlikely that the reduction of Sgo1 and Rts1 at centromeres during anaphase I contributes to the premature loss of centromeric cohesin.
source: It is thus unlikely that the reduction of Sgo1 and Rts1 at centromeres during anaphase I contributes to the premature loss of centromeric cohesin.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the reduction is a consequence of cohesin loss.

claim: Premature expression of CLB3 interferes with Sgo1-PP2A function, but not localization.
source: These findings, together with our observation that centromeric Rec8 phosphorylation is increased in CUP-CLB3 cells, indicate that Sgo1-PP2A function, but not localization, is impaired in CUP-CLB3 cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Sgo1-PP2A localizes normally but centromeric Rec8 phosphorylation is increased.

claim: Both CLB3 and CLB4 induce spindle formation in prophase I.
source: Both cyclins induce spindle formation in prophase I.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Chromosomes are able to attach to the spindle and experience pulling forces only in CUP-CLB3 cells.
source: However, chromosomes are able to attach to this spindle and experience pulling forces only in CUP-CLB3 cells.
evidence: This is supported by data showing sister kinetochore splitting in CUP-CLB3 but not CUP-CLB4 cells.

claim: The ability to form tension-generating attachments correlates with defects in meiosis I chromosome morphogenesis and segregation.
source: Thus, the ability to form tension-generating attachments (i.e. CUP-CLB1 or CUP-CLB3 cells) correlates with defects in meiosis I chromosome morphogenesis and segregation.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing phenotypes of different CUP-CLB strains.

claim: Premature microtubule–kinetochore engagement during premeiotic S phase/early prophase I is the underlying cause of chromosome missegregation in CUP-CLB3 cells.
source: This correlation suggests that premature microtubule–kinetochore engagement during premeiotic S phase/early prophase I is the underlying cause of chromosome missegregation in CUP-CLB3 cells
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between microtubule-kinetochore interactions and chromosome missegregation.

claim: Tension generating microtubule–kinetochore attachments should inhibit meiosis I chromosome morphogenesis.
source: and predicts that tension generating microtubule–kinetochore attachments should inhibit meiosis I chromosome morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the correlation observed.

claim: Preventing microtubule-kinetochore interactions should enable building a proper meiosis I chromosome architecture.
source: Conversely, preventing them should enable building a proper meiosis I chromosome architecture.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the correlation observed.

claim: Overexpression of MAM1 and CDC5 upon a pheromone-induced G1 arrest is sufficient to induce cosegregation of sister chromatids in mitotic anaphase.
source: Overexpression of MAM1 and CDC5 upon a pheromone-induced G1 arrest is sufficient to induce cosegregation of sister chromatids in mitotic anaphase (Monje-Casas et al., 2007, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Monje-Casas et al., 2007 and data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: When cells are allowed to form microtubule–kinetochore attachments prior to CDC5 and MAM1 expression, cosegregation of sister chromatids is prevented.
source: However, when cells are allowed to form microtubule–kinetochore attachments prior to CDC5 and MAM1 expression, cosegregation of sister chromatids is prevented.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Disrupting microtubule–kinetochore interactions by depolymerizing microtubules with nocodazole during the metaphase arrest resulted in robust cosegregation of sister chromatids in anaphase (48% cosegregation).
source: Importantly, disrupting microtubule–kinetochore interactions by depolymerizing microtubules with nocodazole during the metaphase arrest resulted in robust cosegregation of sister chromatids in anaphase (48% cosegregation, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Microtubule–kinetochore interactions modulate the ability of monopolin to induce sister chromatid cosegregation.
source: These results show that microtubule–kinetochore interactions modulate the ability of monopolin to induce sister chromatid cosegregation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that disrupting microtubule-kinetochore interactions allows monopolin to induce cosegregation.

claim: Transient inactivation of microtubule–kinetochore interactions by inactivating the outer kinetochore allowed coorientation factors to associate with kinetochores, despite CLB3 misexpression.
source: The observation that the transient disruption of microtubule–kinetochore interactions, either by inactivating the outer kinetochore or by microtubule depolymerization, allowed coorientation factors to associate with kinetochores, despite CLB3 misexpression, led us to conclude that it is premature microtubule–kinetochore interactions that interfere with the establishment of sister kinetochore coorientation during meiosis I.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that ndc80-1 suppresses the monopolin localization defect in CUP-CLB3 cells (Figure 5C).

claim: Transient inactivation of Ndc80 restored Lrs4 association with kinetochores in CUP-CLB3 cells.
source: Remarkably, CUP-CLB3 ndc80-1 cells showed near wild-type levels of Lrs4 association with kinetochores (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by chromosome spread data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Transient inactivation of Ndc80 restored Lrs4 phosphorylation in CUP-CLB3 cells.
source: Transient inactivation of Ndc80 also restored Lrs4 phosphorylation in CUP-CLB3 cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Premature microtubule–kinetochore interactions prevent sister kinetochore coorientation by disrupting proper localization of the monopolin complex.
source: Our results demonstrate that premature microtubule–kinetochore interactions prevent sister kinetochore coorientation by disrupting proper localization of the monopolin complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that disrupting microtubule-kinetochore interactions restores monopolin localization.

claim: Lrs4 hyperphosphorylation occurs not at the time of nucleolar release, but once Lrs4 localizes to kinetochores.
source: The finding that transient disruption of microtubule–kinetochore interactions also suppresses the Lrs4 phosphorylation defect of CUP-CLB3 cells, furthermore suggests that Lrs4 hyperphosphorylation occurs not at the time of nucleolar release, but once Lrs4 localizes to kinetochores.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that disrupting microtubule-kinetochore interactions restores Lrs4 phosphorylation.

claim: Disrupting microtubule–kinetochore interactions at the time of Clb3 expression caused a considerable increase in the percentage of CUP-CLB3 cells that retained Rec8 around centromeres during anaphase I.
source: Remarkably, disrupting microtubule–kinetochore interactions at the time of Clb3 expression caused a considerable increase in the percentage of CUP-CLB3 cells that retained Rec8 around centromeres during anaphase I (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by chromosome spread data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Restoring centromeric cohesin protection and sister kinetochore coorientation to CUP-CLB3 cells by transient inactivation of Ndc80 restored homolog segregation during meiosis I.
source: Finally, restoring centromeric cohesin protection and sister kinetochore coorientation to CUP-CLB3 cells by transient inactivation of Ndc80 restored homolog segregation during meiosis I (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: This is supported by GFP dot segregation data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplements 2–4.

claim: Similar results were obtained with a temperature sensitive allele of the gene encoding the outer kinetochore component Dam1 (dam1-1) or by disrupting microtubule–kinetochore interactions by benomyl treatment.
source: Similar results were obtained with a temperature sensitive allele of the gene encoding the outer kinetochore component Dam1 (dam1-1) or by disrupting microtubule–kinetochore interactions by benomyl treatment (Figure 5—figure supplements 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 5 and 6.

claim: A striking improvement in overall chromosome segregation and spore viability was observed in CUP-CLB3 ndc80-1 compared to CUP-CLB3 cells.
source: We further observed a striking improvement in overall chromosome segregation and spore viability in CUP-CLB3 ndc80-1 compared to CUP-CLB3 cells (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5G,H.

claim: The suppression of chromosome missegregation in CUP-CLB3 ndc80-1 cells did not depend on the spindle assembly checkpoint.
source: The suppression of chromosome missegregation in CUP-CLB3 ndc80-1 cells did not depend on the spindle assembly checkpoint, because deletion of MAD3 had no discernable effect on the extent of ndc80-1 mediated suppression (Figure 5—figure supplements 7 and 8)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 7 and 8.

claim: The suppression of chromosome missegregation in CUP-CLB3 ndc80-1 cells was not due to the ndc80-1 allele lowering Clb3-CDK activity.
source: nor was it due to the ndc80-1 allele lowering Clb3-CDK activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 9.

claim: The defects associated with CUP-CLB3 cells are due to premature microtubule–kinetochore interactions.
source: In summary, our results demonstrate that the defects associated with CUP-CLB3 cells are due to premature microtubule–kinetochore interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that disrupting microtubule-kinetochore interactions suppresses the defects.

claim: Preventing microtubule–kinetochore interactions during premeiotic S phase and prophase I is necessary to establish a meiosis I-specific chromosome architecture.
source: Our results further suggest that preventing microtubule–kinetochore interactions during premeiotic S phase and prophase I is necessary to establish a meiosis I-specific chromosome architecture.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that premature microtubule-kinetochore interactions disrupt meiosis I chromosome architecture.

claim: The timing of CLB3 induction had an impact on the extent of sister chromatid segregation in meiosis I.
source: We initially noticed that the timing of CLB3 induction had an impact on the extent of sister chromatid segregation in meiosis I, especially in experiments that employed the NDT80 block-release system.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The extent of meiosis I sister chromatid segregation declined as CLB3 was expressed later during the NDT80 block.
source: We observed that the extent of meiosis I sister chromatid segregation declined as CLB3 was expressed later during the NDT80 block (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Previous studies in fission yeast demonstrated that a subset of outer kinetochore components dissociates from the kinetochore during prophase I.
source: Kinetochore components are good candidates for such additional factors, because previous studies in fission yeast demonstrated that a subset of outer kinetochore components dissociates from the kinetochore during prophase I (Asakawa et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Asakawa et al., 2005.

claim: Cluster analysis of kinetochore components revealed two major expression classes: one that peaks in expression prior to or during prophase I (early class), and another that shows peak expression during the meiotic divisions (late class).
source: This analysis revealed two major expression classes, one included kinetochore components that peak in expression prior to or during prophase I (early class), and the other contained components that instead show peak expression during the meiotic divisions (late class).
evidence: This is supported by cluster analysis data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The early class of kinetochore components was enriched for inner kinetochore components (16 of 23).
source: The early class was enriched for inner kinetochore components (16 of 23)
evidence: This is supported by cluster analysis data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The late class of kinetochore components included primarily outer kinetochore components (13 of 18).
source: while the late class included primarily outer kinetochore components (13 of 18) (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplements 1–10).
evidence: This is supported by cluster analysis data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplements 1–10.

claim: The temporal difference in expression suggests that the inner kinetochore is assembled prior to the meiotic divisions, while the outer kinetochore is constructed only as cells enter the meiotic divisions.
source: The temporal difference in expression suggests that the inner kinetochore is assembled prior to the meiotic divisions, while the outer kinetochore is constructed only as cells enter the meiotic divisions.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal expression patterns of kinetochore components.

claim: NDC80 and HSK3 displayed the most differential expression prior to meiosis I and during meiosis I, with a 9.02 and 2.64-fold induction, respectively.
source: Among the outer kinetochore components that displayed peak synthesis during the divisions, NDC80 and a subunit of the DASH complex, HSK3, displayed the most differential expression prior to meiosis I and during meiosis I, with a 9.02 and 2.64-fold induction, respectively (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 6B–D.

claim: Ndc80 levels declined during premeiotic S phase and became undetectable during late prophase I.
source: Ndc80 levels declined during premeiotic S phase and became undetectable during late prophase I (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The ability of CUP-CLB3 to induce sister-chromatid segregation during meiosis I tightly correlated with Ndc80 protein levels.
source: Importantly, the ability of CUP-CLB3 to induce sister-chromatid segregation during meiosis I tightly correlated with Ndc80 protein levels; as Ndc80 protein declines, so does CLB3-induced meiosis I sister chromatid segregation (compare Figure 6A,E).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing Ndc80 protein levels with the extent of sister chromatid segregation.

claim: Hsk3 protein levels were also low until meiosis I entry.
source: Hsk3 protein levels were also low until meiosis I entry (Figure 6F)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Not all outer kinetochore components exhibited a decline in protein levels during prophase I.
source: but not all outer kinetochore components exhibited this decline in protein levels.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing that Ask1 and Dam1 levels do not decline.

claim: Ask1, a subunit of the DASH complex, was present throughout prophase I.
source: For example, Ask1, a subunit of the DASH complex, was present throughout prophase I
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 11.

claim: Levels of another DASH complex component, Dam1, increased during prophase I.
source: and levels of another DASH complex component, Dam1, increased during prophase I (Figure 6—figure supplement 11).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 11.

claim: The assembly of the outer kinetochore is restricted prior to NDT80 expression and pachytene exit due to low levels of a subset of outer kinetochore components.
source: Our findings indicate that the assembly of the outer kinetochore is restricted prior to NDT80 expression and pachytene exit due to low levels of a subset of outer kinetochore components.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some outer kinetochore components are downregulated during prophase I.

claim: Expression of NDC80 and/or HSK3 alone caused only a few cells to recruit Ask1 to kinetochores.
source: Whereas expression of either gene alone caused only a few cells to recruit Ask1 to kinetochores
evidence: This is supported by chromosome spread data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: Cells simultaneously expressing NDC80, HSK3 and CLB3 during prophase I showed colocalization between Ask1 and the inner kinetochore component Ndc10, to an equal or greater extent than what was observed in metaphase I-arrested wild-type cells.
source: cells simultaneously expressing NDC80, HSK3 and CLB3 during prophase I showed colocalization between Ask1 and the inner kinetochore component Ndc10, to an equal or greater extent than what was observed in metaphase I-arrested wild-type cells (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by chromosome spread data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: Induction of CLB3 gave rise to bipolar spindles that appeared fragile with a weakened midzone.
source: In addition, induction of CLB3 under the conditions mentioned above gave rise to bipolar spindles that appeared fragile with a weakened midzone.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8D,E.

claim: Coexpression of CLB3, HSK3 and NDC80 resulted in the formation of robust bipolar spindles.
source: In contrast, consistent with stable microtubule–kinetochore interactions, coexpression of CLB3, HSK3 and NDC80 resulted in the formation of robust bipolar spindles (Figure 8D,E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8D,E.

claim: The expression of NDC80 and/or HSK3 during an NDT80 block caused a considerable increase in meiosis I sister chromatid segregation in CUP-CLB3 cells.
source: Importantly, the expression of NDC80 and/or HSK3 during an NDT80 block caused a considerable increase in meiosis I sister chromatid segregation in CUP-CLB3 cells (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is supported by GFP dot segregation data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Under conditions in which CLB3 expression alone failed to induce meiosis I sister chromatid segregation, expression of CLB3 together with NDC80 and HSK3 caused a substantial increase in meiosis I sister chromatid segregation.
source: Furthermore, under conditions in which CLB3 expression alone failed to induce meiosis I sister chromatid segregation, expression of CLB3 together with NDC80 and HSK3 caused a substantial increase in meiosis I sister chromatid segregation (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is supported by GFP dot segregation data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Expression of CLB3 together with NDC80 and HSK3 caused sister chromatid segregation in meiosis I even when cells were maintained in a prolonged NDT80 block prior to expression.
source: This occurred even when cells were maintained in a prolonged NDT80 block prior to expression of CLB3, NDC80 and HSK3 (Figure 9)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Limiting outer kinetochore assembly is an additional mechanism to prevent microtubule–kinetochore interactions during premeiotic S phase and prophase I.
source: We conclude that limiting outer kinetochore assembly is an additional mechanism to prevent microtubule–kinetochore interactions during premeiotic S phase and prophase I.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that expressing outer kinetochore components enhances CLB3-induced sister chromatid segregation.

claim: Premature expression of CLB3 interferes with establishment of the meiosis I chromosome segregation pattern by inducing premature microtubule–kinetochore engagement.
source: How does premature expression of CLB3 interfere with establishment of the meiosis I chromosome segregation pattern? The comparison of the effects caused by CLB3 and CLB4 misexpression provided insight into this question.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of CLB3 and CLB4 phenotypes.

claim: Premature microtubule–kinetochore engagement during premeiotic S phase/early prophase I is the underlying cause of chromosome missegregation in CUP-CLB3 cells.
source: This correlation suggests that premature microtubule–kinetochore engagement during premeiotic S phase/early prophase I is the underlying cause of chromosome missegregation in CUP-CLB3 cells
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between microtubule-kinetochore interactions and chromosome missegregation.

claim: Restriction of cyclin-CDK activity during premeiotic S phase and prophase I appears to be the major mechanism preventing premature microtubule–kinetochore interactions.
source: Restriction of cyclin-CDK activity during premeiotic S phase and prophase I appears to be the major mechanism preventing premature microtubule–kinetochore interactions, but our data indicate that regulation of outer kinetochore assembly serves as an additional mechanism to prevent this from occurring.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cyclin misexpression causes premature microtubule-kinetochore interactions.

claim: Regulation of outer kinetochore assembly serves as an additional mechanism to prevent premature microtubule–kinetochore interactions.
source: Restriction of cyclin-CDK activity during premeiotic S phase and prophase I appears to be the major mechanism preventing premature microtubule–kinetochore interactions, but our data indicate that regulation of outer kinetochore assembly serves as an additional mechanism to prevent this from occurring.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that outer kinetochore components are downregulated during prophase I.

claim: CUP-CLB3 can only induce meiosis I sister chromatid segregation when expressed during premeiotic S phase/early prophase I, but fails to do so when expressed during late prophase I.
source: CUP-CLB3 can only induce meiosis I sister chromatid segregation when expressed during premeiotic S phase/early prophase I, but fails to do so when expressed during late prophase I.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The difference in CLB3's ability to induce sister chromatid segregation is likely due to the outer kinetochore being present only until early prophase I.
source: This difference is likely due to the outer kinetochore being present only until early prophase I.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between outer kinetochore presence and CLB3's ability to induce sister chromatid segregation.

claim: The presence of Clb3-CDKs alone during late prophase I is not sufficient to cause meiosis I sister chromatid segregation but outer kinetochore components must also be expressed.
source: This result demonstrates that the presence of Clb3-CDKs alone during late prophase I is not sufficient to cause meiosis I sister chromatid segregation but that outer kinetochore components must also be expressed.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that coexpression of CLB3, NDC80, and HSK3 induces sister chromatid segregation when CLB3 alone does not.

claim: In budding yeast, two essential components of the outer kinetochore, Ndc80 and Hsk3, are downregulated during prophase I.
source: In budding yeast, two essential components of the outer kinetochore, Ndc80 and Hsk3, are downregulated during prophase I.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: In S. pombe, Ndc80 and its binding partner Nuf2 dissociate from kinetochores in prophase I.
source: In S. pombe, Ndc80 and its binding partner Nuf2 dissociate from kinetochores in prophase I (Asakawa et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Asakawa et al., 2005.

claim: Deconstruction of the outer kinetochore may be a conserved feature of meiotic prophase I.
source: raising the interesting possibility that deconstruction of the outer kinetochore is a conserved feature of meiotic prophase I.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on observations in budding yeast and fission yeast.

claim: In S. pombe, Ndc80 and Nuf2 dissociation from kinetochores depends on the mating pheromone signaling pathway.
source: This dissociation depends on the mating pheromone signaling pathway (Asakawa et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Asakawa et al., 2005.

claim: Ectopic induction of meiosis without mating pheromone signaling (i.e. in pat1 mutants) results in segregation of sister chromatids instead of homologous chromosomes in meiosis I.
source: Intriguingly, ectopic induction of meiosis without mating pheromone signaling (i.e. in pat1 mutants), results in segregation of sister chromatids instead of homologous chromosomes in meiosis I (Yamamoto and Hiraoka, 2003; Yamamoto et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yamamoto and Hiraoka, 2003 and Yamamoto et al., 2004.

claim: The change in the pattern of chromosome segregation in pat1 mutants may arise from premature microtubule–kinetochore interactions due to a defect in outer kinetochore disassembly.
source: Perhaps this change in the pattern of chromosome segregation in pat1 mutants arises from premature microtubule–kinetochore interactions due to a defect in outer kinetochore disassembly.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observations in pat1 mutants.

claim: In mouse oocytes, the Ndc80 complex is recruited to chromosomes only after nuclear envelope breakdown.
source: Interestingly, in mouse oocytes, the Ndc80 complex is recruited to chromosomes only after nuclear envelope breakdown (Sun et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sun et al., 2011.

claim: Outer kinetochore assembly may also be prevented in meiotic prophase I in vertebrates.
source: raising the possibility that outer kinetochore assembly is also prevented in meiotic prophase I in vertebrates.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on observations in mouse oocytes.

claim: Errors in chromosome segregation during meiosis result in aneuploidy, the leading cause of birth defects and miscarriages in humans.
source: Errors in chromosome segregation during meiosis result in aneuploidy, the leading cause of birth defects and miscarriages in humans (Hassold and Hunt, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hassold and Hunt, 2001.

claim: The establishment of a meiosis-specific chromosome segregation pattern depends on the regulation of microtubule–kinetochore interactions.
source: We discovered that the establishment of a meiosis-specific chromosome segregation pattern depends on the regulation of microtubule–kinetochore interactions.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Regulation of microtubule–kinetochore interactions is achieved by regulating cyclin-CDK activity as well as assembly of the outer kinetochore.
source: This is achieved by regulating cyclin-CDK activity as well as assembly of the outer kinetochore.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that both mechanisms contribute to preventing premature microtubule-kinetochore interactions.

claim: There is evidence for similar regulatory events across different organisms.
source: There is evidence for similar regulatory events across different organisms (Asakawa et al., 2005; Sugimura and Lilly, 2006; Biedermann et al., 2009; Von Stetina and Orr-Weaver, 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in other organisms.

claim: Temporal restriction of microtubule-kinetochore interactions is an evolutionarily conserved event required to execute proper meiotic chromosome segregation.
source: suggesting that temporal restriction of microtubule-kinetochore interactions is an evolutionarily conserved event required to execute proper meiotic chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that similar regulatory events occur in different organisms.
